rv.q: In the end, Stanley will have his awful, violent revenge on Blanche. She will see it coming — she'll struggle, her eyes will go wide like a deer's and she'll try to bolt. But he'll get her and then he will surely break her. What the races are of the actors on stage is immaterial.
As good as it looks, the visceral production style does come at the cost of psychological subtlety.
Handsomely designed by a top-flight team — including Eugene Lee (set), Paul Tazewell (costumes) and Edward Pierce (lighting) — this “Streetcar” is mostly an exquisite snooze.
More important, Underwood adds an unexpected vulnerability that makes Stanley’s violence as explosive and, oddly, as believable, as any I’ve seen.
Without that kind of energy “Streetcar” can’t run at its max but just rattle along.

On that basis, the revival of the 1947 "Streetcar" – set, for some reason, in 1952 – is a disappointment, undone by several one-note characterizations.
The result is embarrassing and sad.

cn.t: Mixed reviews greet this multiracial revival, with critics praising the powerhouse performances and sexual magnetism of Underwood and Parker, but divided on Mann's direction—some find it accessible and moving, others criticize it as torpid and misguided.

vs.sum: One of Broadway's least comfortable theaters, with notoriously tight legroom and narrow seats. The lack of rake means tall patrons in front block your view. Restrooms are in the basement, creating long intermission lines. For legroom, target Row A or N in Orchestra.

acc.note: 6 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No steps from sidewalk. Infrared devices available.
